issues.item: Fear of Rage: I will not be able to control my anger and will do something terrible
issues.explanation: The profile is centered on witnessed trauma with triggers involving crowded places, conversation topics, and bus riding, plus appraisals of vigilance and outsider status. The anger-loss-of-control appraisal introduces a distinct perpetration/impulse-control theme that is not supported by the other selected triggers, memory, threat, or strategy items, making it clinically hard to place within the same formulation.

Avoiding sex is not well linked to the rest of the profile. There are no sexual trauma cues, intimacy-related triggers, body-related appraisals, or threat/memory items that would explain sex-specific avoidance. Relative to the rest of the selected items, this strategy appears disconnected and inconsistent with the formulation.

vignette:
Dorothy is a 72-year-old network engineer who still works full-time, managing the infrastructure of a large urban hospital. Seven months ago, while riding the bus home, she witnessed a young man collapse and die of an overdose in the seat across from her. The scene was chaotic—passengers shouted, the driver pulled over, paramedics arrived too late—and Dorothy sat frozen, watching, unable to look away. She later learned the man had been revived, but what she saw that evening never left her: the blue pallor, the glassy eyes, the frantic bystanders. In the weeks afterward, she found herself avoiding the bus stop altogether, walking an extra mile to catch a different line, and eventually driving instead—an expense that strained her budget. She also stopped going to the grocery store at peak hours and declined invitations to her grandson’s crowded school events. She told herself she was just being sensible.

But the vigilance grew. Dorothy began to feel that she had to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next. On the rare occasions she did enter a crowded space—say, the hospital cafeteria at lunchtime—she would scan every face, every hand, every exit, and the world felt terrifyingly unpredictable. Each instance of crowding or bus riding reinforced her belief that the world is a dangerous place, and that belief, in turn, made her more alert to potential threats in those same environments. She started to notice certain conversation topics at work—any discussion of illness, death, or even public transportation—and would feel a surge of anxiety, interpreting them as reminders that danger lurked everywhere. Her colleagues noticed she had become distant, and she quietly felt like she had become permanently an outsider now, separated from others who did not seem to live under the same shadow.

To manage these feelings, Dorothy adopted a strategy of forcing herself to think only positive thoughts whenever a trigger arose. If a bus rumbled past her window, she would mentally replace the image with a pleasant memory of her garden. If a coworker mentioned a recent emergency room visit, she would silently recite reassuring phrases: *Everything is fine, I am safe.* But the effort of positive reframing did not reduce her hypervigilance; instead, it left her more exhausted and more convinced that the world required constant mental management. And the more she avoided crowds and the event site—she had not walked past the bus stop where the incident occurred since that day—the more isolated she became, reinforcing the sense that she was different, marked, an outsider. Her avoidance also made her more sensitive to triggers when they were unavoidable, because each avoided situation confirmed that the trigger was genuinely dangerous.

The causal cycle tightened over months. Crowded places triggered her negative appraisals of the world as dangerous, and those appraisals drove her to avoid crowds even more. Her avoidance, in turn, made her less practiced in managing ordinary anxiety, so any brush with a trigger—a full bus passing by, a coworker’s casual mention of a medical emergency—felt catastrophic, further cementing her vigilance. She began planning her entire day around preventing exposure, checking traffic cameras at home to see how full the buses were before even leaving the house. Her husband grew concerned; she snapped at him once when he suggested she just take the bus for a short errand. She felt she could not explain why it felt impossible—why her body reacted before her mind could even form a thought.

What finally brought Dorothy to seek help was a morning when she could not bring herself to enter the hospital building because a maintenance van was parked near the entrance, blocking the automatic doors and reminding her of the ambulance that had blocked the bus that evening. She stood outside for twenty minutes, heart racing, then turned around and drove home. That afternoon she called a therapist. She is afraid that the world will never feel safe again, and she is hoping—though she cannot quite say it aloud—that someone can help her stop fighting the same invisible battle every day.
